about: How the outcome web runs on the new core (src/core2/modules/outcome-web.ts). The links themselves, their sizes, shapes, lags and sources are data/research/outcome-web/links.json; each place outcome's real starting level is data/research/outcome-web/place-outcome-bases-2024.json; who each link reaches is data/research/outcome-web/landing-plan.json with the age cohorts in person-recipient-age-cohorts.json. This file holds only what those leave open: when the web runs each month, the outcomes it keeps that have no per-state base file, the records the engines already keep that it reads, the recipient rules as selectors over core2 records, and who must provide each missing measure.

links.anchor: Negligence-standard child access prevention laws (an adult is liable when a child can get an unsecured gun) went with 13% fewer firearm deaths among children 0 to 14 from 1991 to 2016, and 12 to 15% fewer firearm homicides, suicides and accidental deaths; weaker recklessness laws showed no effect. RAND rates the evidence supportive. The range is the default 25% spread.
links.source: Azad et al. 2020 (JAMA Pediatrics); RAND Science of Gun Policy, 5th ed.
links.notes: Unsupported until a producer computes youth firearm deaths: the cause is now a state's law on responsibility for unsecured guns near children, a question the game asks, but youth firearm deaths are not a kept place outcome.

links.per: adoption of statutory public-place stand-your-ground law versus no such adoption in the controlled pooled study
links.anchor: Increases firearm homicides (RAND: supportive)
links.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8861849/
why: The study associates statutory stand-your-ground adoption with higher monthly firearm-homicide rates after controlling for comparison states, seasonality and long-term trends.
Its treatment is an extension of legal immunity for lethal self-defense outside the home to places where a person has a legal right to be.

That legal change can alter the perceived legal consequences of choosing lethal force. The authors describe possible encouragement of otherwise avoidable deadly encounters; deterrence is the competing explanation.

A person chooses whether to use lethal force in a particular encounter from the situation and their own record. A firearm discharge can physically kill another person. The aggregate estimate does not choose that action or victim.
Legal rule: statutory protection for qualifying public-place self-defense; physical fact: lethal force can kill. Actual behavioral mediation is not identified by this study.

conditions.strongerWeakerAbsent: Large increases in total/firearm homicide associations cluster in several Southern states; reported combined outcome increases16.2%–33.5%. Some states have no statistically significant associations. That combined range is not a firearm-only numerical interval.
conditions.rangeMeaning: [0.03,0.13] is the published95%interval around the pooled firearm-homicide rate ratio minus1. It is not a distribution of local effects, not a bound on every state, and not a territory transport estimate.
conditions.transportMissing: Numerical firearm-only state-specific estimates and their intervals fromFigure3/supplement, plus evidence for later-adopting and excluded places. No universal state-specific effect is claimed.
conditions.mediationLimit: The legal treatment and aggregate association are measured in the paper. The psychological pathway is an authors-discussed hypothesis, not measured person-level mediation or proof of a particular encounter.

reverseOnRepeal.reason: The treatment analyzed is adoption during2000–2016; no repeal experiment or repeal estimate is supplied. Prior deaths cannot reverse. Future encounters require the actual replacement law and effective date. Do not negate0.08 or invert1.08 as a researched repeal effect.

who.studyPopulation: Forty-one US states during1999–2017:23 statutory adopters and18 controls; statewide monthly firearm-homicide deaths per100000people. The dataset includes170659firearm homicides.
who.exclusions: Nine states excluded:Utah/Iowa lacked sufficient timing/data;seven had case-law stand-your-ground principles, contaminating comparison. No territory, county-specific, township-specific or individual exposed-defendant estimate.
who.legalCoverage: People in qualifying public-place self-defense encounters under operative law; the study definition is not a grant of authority to local governments or proof every homicide involved a self-defense claim.

lagWhy.measured: Methods model a step change in monthly statewide rates at statutory enactment, adjusted for seasonality and state trends, with at least12months before/after for included adopters.
lagWhy.lagInterpretation: lagMonths0 describes that monthly aggregate model specification; it is not a measured immediate personal reaction or zero procedural delay. No separate distributed-lag coefficient is supplied.

links.researchActivationLimit: The cause is now the law in force on the stand-your-ground question (law:us-policy-positions:justice-public-safety.stand-your-ground), so this coefficient acts when a state adopts. The research establishes adoption only, so a repeal is held at no effect (floor 1), not at the opposite of 0.08. Applying it to places beyond the study's 41 states, and enabling this reader at all, still need review before the number is called settled.

links.anchor: States that limited handgun sales to people 21 and older had an 18% lower suicide rate among 18- to 20-year-olds from 2001 to 2017, nearly 2 fewer suicides per 100,000 at those ages. The study reports suicide by all means, so the firearm share is an assumption; provisional. The range is the default 25% spread. RAND rates the evidence supportive.
links.source: Raifman et al. 2020 (BMJ); RAND Science of Gun Policy, 5th ed.
links.notes: Unsupported until a producer computes youth firearm suicide: the cause is now a state's law on a handgun buying age of 21, a question the game asks, but youth firearm suicide is not a kept place outcome.

links.anchor: The 2005 fine-particle nonattainment designations lowered PM2.5 by an estimated 0.34 micrograms per cubic meter (95% posterior interval -1.54 to +0.69) against a baseline of 14.48 in nonattainment counties, about -2.3% (-10.7% to +4.8%). Plain before-and-after comparisons give about -1.6 micrograms, but overstate it because dirtier places were already improving faster. Clean Air Act rules for coarser particulates in the 1970s cut them more clearly (Chay and Greenstone 2003).
links.source: Zigler, Choirat and Dominici 2018 (Epidemiology); Chay and Greenstone 2003
links.notes: The cause is a state's law on a clean-up plan for counties that fail the federal soot and dust standards. A state starts at yes when the EPA Green Book (September 30, 2026) lists one of its counties as nonattainment for PM-2.5 or PM-10.

links.anchor: CBO: the 2025 law's community engagement requirement adds 5.3 million uninsured by 2034. It applies to expansion adults, so it falls on expansion states: about 16.4 million uninsured there in 2024, so about +32%. Arkansas 2018: nearly 1 in 4 of those subject lost coverage within months, mostly over paperwork.
links.source: CBO supplemental estimate for Public Law 119-21 (2025); Sommers et al. 2019 (NEJM)
why: The law adds work or exemption conditions to coverage.
A recipient must satisfy and document those conditions.
Recorded failure or administrative loss can end coverage.
The terminal is a legal eligibility decision or paperwork process, not a presumed decision to avoid work.
links.conditions: Preserve the existing per-world/per-place draw and recorded range where present. Statutory reach, actual eligible people and service capacity differ; no blanket state coverage is inferred.
links.reverseOnRepeal: Remove or replace the current legal exposure prospectively; enrollment, services, contracts and accumulated outcomes need their own records, not an immediate numerical inverse.

why: A funded preschool place can provide care during specific hours.

That coverage can make a particular job schedule feasible.

Bedrock is actual child care and a parent hiring decision, not a participation multiplier choosing employment.

strongerWhen: The parent had binding care costs/schedule constraints and an accessible job.
weakerWhen: The household already had equivalent care or only part-day care is provided.
absentWhen: No preschool place, child enrollment, usable schedule or feasible job exists.

links.lagWhy: The existing12-month lag represents enrollment and labor response. Verify the D.C./Quebec study time window and whether the effect is percentage points or a relative participation change.

links.anchor: Boston's universal preschool: +6 points on-time graduation for children who enrolled; with about 70% enrolled, about +5% of a state's rate, 14 years after the first four-year-olds. Tennessee's program did worse; quality decides where in the range a world lands.
links.source: Gray-Lobe, Pathak and Walters 2023; Vanderbilt TN-VPK
why: A preschool program offers a place with particular instructional quality.
A child obtains the educational exposure only through actual enrollment and attendance.
The instruction and later school context can alter skills and persistence.
The exposed cohort reaches the age and requirements for high-school completion years later.
Bedrock is child attendance followed by completed schooling; quality differences explain why program studies need separate conditions.

strongerWhen: The funded program provides the quality and population exposure of the favorable study.
weakerWhen: Program quality, follow-on schooling or participant share differs from that study.
absentWhen: The child does not attend or is not yet old enough for the measured completion outcome.

links.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal ends future offered places. It cannot delete an earlier child exposure or a completed diploma; the already exposed cohort may retain long-term effects.
links.who: Actual enrolled preschool cohorts as they reach high-school age; not present-day adults or all children in the state.
links.lagWhy: The existing168-month lag follows four-year-olds toward high-school graduation. It is fourteen years, so a24-month audit must report not-yet-due rather than missing firing.

links.anchor: Illinois ended cash bail in September 2023: within a year pretrial jail populations fell about 14% in Cook and the collar counties and about 25% in rural counties; people still held three days after arrest fell from 33% to 9% of defendants. New Jersey nearly ended money bail in 2017: pretrial jail population down 43.9% from 2015 to 2018, part of it before the reform; MDRC found detention below the pre-reform trend. Before-and-after counts, not a controlled estimate, so provisional.
links.source: Loyola University Chicago Center for Criminal Justice 2024 (Illinois Pretrial Fairness Act, first year); New Jersey Judiciary 2018 Criminal Justice Reform Report to the Governor and Legislature; MDRC 2019 New Jersey pretrial evaluation
links.notes: Not hooked by design: the justice code already decides each defendant's detention from the bail law in force, so a pretrial-detained place rate would count the law twice.

links.anchor: Across 50 states from 1991 to 2015, shall-issue carry laws (permits on demand) went with 8.6% higher firearm homicide (rate ratio 1.086, about 1.047 to 1.125), 6.5% higher total homicide and 10.6% higher handgun homicide than may-issue laws; RAND rates shall-issue raising homicide as supportive. A permit required, read as the stricter side, is about -8% (1/1.086). Provisional because the study compares shall-issue with may-issue, not a permit with no permit.
links.source: Siegel et al. 2017 (AJPH); RAND Science of Gun Policy, 5th ed.

links.anchor: No effect on registration either, for any group
links.source: Cantoni and Pons 2021 (QJE)

links.per: law in force: about +1 point on a turnout near 66% of eligible voters
links.anchor: AVR raises registration a lot; the new registrants vote less often than others, but enough of them vote to raise the eligible turnout rate, and the effect builds the longer AVR is in place. Front-end registration (at the agency visit) raised turnout 1.1 points and back-end registration (a notice after the visit) 3.3 points, as Data for Progress quotes the paper; the front-end size is used, with the back-end one as the top of the range. For people whose registration AVR updated when they moved, turnout rose 5.8 points (Orange County, California), which bounds it from above.
links.source: McGhee, Hill and Romero 2021, The Registration and Turnout Effects of Automatic Voter Registration (SSRN 3933442); Kim 2021, APSA preprint (doi 10.33774/apsa-2021-3wzbh)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0); zero where the place already restores the vote by the end of a sentence
links.group: people barred from voting after their sentence
links.anchor: Restoring the vote at the end of a sentence adds people to the voting-eligible population who vote less than others, so the eligible turnout rate falls while ballots rise. Each place's size is (1 + s x t / T) / (1 + s) - 1: s is its share of the voting-eligible population barred after their sentence, t = 0.14 the turnout of restored people (0.12 to 0.22 for the range) and T its 2024 turnout. In Tennessee the rate falls about 4% while ballots rise about 0.8 points of the old eligible population. The places that already restore by the end of a sentence (the rest of the states, D.C., the territories, and Arkansas, where Locked Out 2024 counts no one barred after the sentence, as Research 3 read it) have no one for the law to restore.
links.source: The Sentencing Project, Locked Out 2024 (post-sentence shares by state); Meredith and Morse, Florida restorations 2007 to 2011 (12 to 16% voted); Burch 2011 (about 22%); University of Florida Election Lab 2024 VEP turnout. Sized by Research 3, 9/29/2026, /mnt/project-files/research/law-effect-sizes/justice.json.

links.anchor: New apartments in large buildings twice as many a year where the law allows more homes. The 1.0 proportional increase is the recorded midpoint calibration: Minneapolis's housing stock grew three times as fast as the rest of Minnesota's from 2017 to 2022 (Pew, January 4, 2024); California's SB 9 approved almost none in its first year (Terner Center, 2022); and Sao Paulo's upzoning added 1.9% to the stock in the long run (Research 1). New buildings then cut nearby rents 5% to 7%.
links.source: Pew Charitable Trusts, January 4, 2024; Terner Center, 2022; Anagol, Ferreira and Rexer 2021, NBER w29440

links.anchor: A represented tenant's chance of eviction -45% to -78%, middle -62%. town-rent.ts already decides each case with the lawyer in it; a producer of housing.eviction counts those recorded cases and never applies this link again
links.source: Cassidy and Currie 2022, NBER w29836; NYC Office of Civil Justice FY2019
links.notes: Not hooked by design: living-world/town-rent.ts already decides each eviction case with the tenant's lawyer present, so a place eviction rate that also applied this link would count the law twice; a producer of housing.eviction should count those recorded cases instead.

links.anchor: Youth Risk Behavior Surveys 1993 to 2017: recreational marijuana laws went with 8% lower odds of teen use in the past 30 days (odds ratio 0.92, 0.87 to 0.96) and 9% lower odds of frequent use; medical marijuana laws showed no change. Single-state studies differ (Washington 8th and 10th graders rose after legal sales), so the size is a small decrease with a range across zero.
links.source: Anderson, Hansen, Rees and Sabia 2019 (JAMA Pediatrics); Cerdá et al. 2017 (JAMA Pediatrics)

links.anchor: Prohibiting payday loans goes with a 35% decline in their use (Urban Institute working paper, read); the published version reports 32%. A state rate cap of 36% APR ends storefront payday lending as a prohibition does. Cross-state survey evidence, not a trial. Read on the count of consumer lenders, a stand-in for use. Enforced loan limits in Dallas and Austin cut payday loan volume 44% and 61% (Wang and Burke 2021, NBER w28765), inside the range; the effect began when enforcement began
links.source: McKernan, Ratcliffe and Kuehn 2010 (Urban Institute) and 2013 (JEBO); Wang and Burke 2021 (NBER w28765) for the range

links.anchor: California paid family leave raised mothers' return to work within a year of a birth (Baum and Ruhm: 13 to 18% more likely among those who worked during pregnancy) and the hours of mothers of 1- to 3-year-olds by about 10 to 17% (Rossin-Slater, Ruhm and Waldfogel), but tax records show first-time mothers' employment 5 to 7% lower up to ten years later (Bailey, Byker, Patel and Ramnath). Short-run gains, long-run losses; the size is small and positive with a range that crosses zero.
links.source: Rossin-Slater, Ruhm and Waldfogel 2013 (JPAM); Baum and Ruhm 2016 (JPAM); Bailey, Byker, Patel and Ramnath 2019 (NBER w26416)

links.anchor: Sweden's carbon tax cut transport emissions almost 11% over 1990 to 2005; British Columbia's cut transport emissions but brought no large, significant fall in total emissions. Transport is about a third of a place's emissions, so the total falls about 3%
links.source: Andersson 2019, American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 11(4); Pretis 2022, Environmental and Resource Economics 83

links.anchor: Before-and-after studies in seven states in the 1970s and 1980s found total litter fell 30 to 64% after a container deposit took effect
links.source: Container Recycling Institute, Bottle Bill Resource Guide, summary of state litter studies (bottlebill.org); the individual studies were not read

links.anchor: Stores raised prices on covered drinks 4% when New York's deposit took in bottled water, and left other prices alone. Drinks bought for home are 1.9% of household spending (2024: $142 billion nonalcoholic and $229 billion alcoholic of $19.9 trillion), about two thirds of it in covered containers, so the whole price level rises about 0.05%
links.source: Consequences of Bottle Bills, Journal of Marketing 2025 (doi 10.1177/00222429251347284), abstract read; Bureau of Economic Analysis, NIPA personal consumption expenditures 2024 (DNBVRC, DAOPRC, DPCERC)

links.anchor: Seven years after passage, renewable portfolio standards left retail electricity prices 11% higher, while cutting the power sector's carbon emissions 11 to 24%
links.source: Greenstone and Nath 2019, Becker Friedman Institute Working Paper 2019-62 (Do Renewable Portfolio Standards Deliver?)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0), in percentage points of beverage containers recycled
links.anchor: States with a deposit law return 71.6% of their beverage containers and states without one 27.9% (43.7 points). Return rates run from 33% under a 5-cent deposit to 92% under a 10-cent one, so the range spans a weak program to a strong one. A new program opens its return points within about six months
links.source: Container Recycling Institute, Bottle Bill Resource Guide (container-recycling.org/bottle-bills), quoting BEAR 2002, and its 2026 table of redemption rates in the 10 deposit states; sized by Research 6 (07 LAW EFFECT SIZES, September 29, 2026)

links.anchor: CBO: $15 by 2025 lifts about 1.3 million people out of poverty, about -3.5% of the poor. Scaled by how far the state's own minimum sits below $15; a state already at $15 is not moved.
links.source: CBO 2019, The Effects on Employment and Family Income of Increasing the Federal Minimum Wage

links.anchor: CBO 2021 (Raise the Wage Act, $15 by 2025): 1.4 million fewer jobs in its central estimate, likely range near zero to 2.7 million, among the 17 million workers who would otherwise earn under $15, so about -8% (0 to -16%). Bunching studies of state raises find little job loss at moderate levels.
links.source: CBO 2021, The Budgetary Effects of the Raise the Wage Act of 2021; CBO 2019; Cengiz, Dube, Lindner and Zipperer 2019 (QJE)
links.notes: Unsupported: the study's 8% is jobs lost among workers who earned under $15, a group a $15 minimum empties by definition, so a state base of jobs paying under $15 would read zero once the law is in force whatever happened to employment; the outcome needs a count of those workers' jobs, which the game does not keep.

links.anchor: Boston: no detectable effect on state test scores; Tennessee: lower scores by 6th grade.
links.source: Gray-Lobe, Pathak and Walters 2023; Vanderbilt TN-VPK
why: A child attends preschool with a particular curriculum and instructional quality.
That exposure changes learning experiences only for the attending child.
Later school instruction can reinforce or offset that experience.
A later math assessment records the skills then acquired.
Bedrock is actual instruction and assessment; adverse Tennessee and null test findings cannot become a universal positive score.

strongerWhen: Program and subsequent schooling resemble the measured comparison.
weakerWhen: Quality or later-school context differs from the evaluated program.
absentWhen: There is no enrolled exposure or no assessment at the relevant follow-up.

links.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal affects future attendance opportunities. It does not erase an assessment or reverse learned skills; subsequent instruction needs its own path.
links.who: Enrolled preschool pupils at the study follow-up ages and programs; statewide dilution remains a separate unverified conversion.
links.lagWhy: The outcome is eighth-grade math. A four-year-old enrolled in the fall takes the eighth-grade test about nine years and nine months later (117 months), the same lag as the reading link (CTO ruling 8).

links.group: children who enrolled, as eighth graders
links.anchor: The studies disagree. Boston's lottery found no reading effect from third grade through tenth (+0.005 standard deviations, ruling out more than +0.12). Georgia and Oklahoma's statewide programs left eighth-grade reading about where it was: +0.8 NAEP points for lower-income children, -0.8 for the rest. Tennessee's randomized program left sixth graders 0.13 standard deviations behind in English. At the 2024 national base near 29% proficient, 0.1 standard deviation is about 12% of the rate, so the range runs from Tennessee (-15%, its offered-versus-not-offered gap) to Boston's upper bound with about 70% enrolled (+10%), centered just below zero. Abecedarian's large adult reading gain (+0.79 standard deviations) came from full-day care from infancy plus school-age help for about 100 children, not a pre-K year, so it is left out of the range.
links.source: Gray-Lobe, Pathak and Walters 2023 (QJE), Table 6; Cascio and Schanzenbach 2013 (Brookings Papers), Table 7; Durkin, Lipsey, Farran and Wiesen 2022 (Developmental Psychology); Campbell et al. 2002 (Abecedarian); Camilli, Vargas, Ryan and Barnett 2010 meta-analysis (NIEER)
why: A child attends preschool with a particular curriculum and instructional quality.
That exposure changes early language and literacy experiences only for the attending child.
Later school instruction can build on, wash out or offset those early gains.
An eighth-grade reading assessment records the skills then acquired.
Bedrock is actual instruction and assessment; early gains that fade by middle school cannot become a universal positive score.

strongerWhen: The program's quality and the later schools resemble settings where gains lasted, and enrolled children come from lower-income homes.
weakerWhen: Quality is low, as in the Tennessee program, or children would have attended a comparable preschool anyway.
absentWhen: There is no enrolled exposure, or the first enrolled cohort has not yet reached eighth grade.

links.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal ends future offered places. It does not erase an assessment or reverse skills an enrolled cohort already learned.
links.who: Enrolled preschool cohorts once they take the eighth-grade reading test; not current students who never had the program.
links.lagWhy: A four-year-old enrolled in the fall takes the eighth-grade test about nine years and nine months later (117 months).

links.anchor: Behavior effects differ by program. Perry Preschool cut violent-crime arrests by age 40 by a third (32% vs. 48%), and Chicago's Child-Parent Centers cut violent juvenile arrests 41% (9.0% vs. 15.3%), both for low-income children. Boston's universal program cut high-school suspensions 36% (0.06 off 0.166) and juvenile incarceration by 0.8 points, a large share of a rare event. Tennessee's program left sixth graders with more discipline problems (0.09 standard deviations more offenses). People under 18 made about 9.8% of violent-crime arrests in 2019. A third fewer offenses among the 70% of teenagers who enrolled moves a state's violent crime about -2.3%. Effects are smaller for better-off children, so the center is about half that; Tennessee sets the top of the range.
links.source: Schweinhart et al. 2005 (Perry Preschool at 40); Reynolds et al. 2001 (JAMA); Gray-Lobe, Pathak and Walters 2023 (QJE), Table 7; Durkin, Lipsey, Farran and Wiesen 2022 (Developmental Psychology); FBI Crime in the United States 2019, arrests by age
why: A child attends preschool where teachers practice self-control, turn-taking and classroom routines.
Those habits can change how the child behaves in school and how often adults discipline the child.
Fewer suspensions and closer ties to school can keep a teenager away from fights and robberies.
Only offenses the teenager actually commits and police record reach the crime count.
Bedrock is a particular teenager's conduct and a recorded offense; the program does not stop a crime by itself.

strongerWhen: Enrolled children come from low-income homes and the program has the quality of the Perry, Chicago or Boston programs.
weakerWhen: Most enrolled children would have attended another preschool, or the program resembles Tennessee's.
absentWhen: The first enrolled cohort has not reached its teens, or no child enrolled.

links.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal ends future offered places. Teenagers who already attended keep whatever habits they formed; later cohorts lose the program.
links.who: Enrolled preschool cohorts once they reach ages 14 to 17; adults and earlier cohorts are untouched.
links.lagWhy: The first enrolled four-year-olds turn 18 fourteen years later (168 months), when every juvenile age group has had the program.

links.anchor: Statewide voucher users lost ground in math at first (Louisiana, Indiana, Ohio), fading after a few years; few students use them, so the state moves little.
links.source: Abdulkadiroglu, Pathak and Walters 2018; Waddington and Berends 2018 (to confirm)
why: A funded award can give an eligible household another school choice.
The household can use it only if an eligible school has a place and the remaining charge/transport is feasible.
Enrollment changes the instruction the pupil actually receives.
That instruction may improve or worsen the skills measured by later math assessments.
Bedrock is a family decision, paid award and school enrollment; private status alone does not imply higher quality.

strongerWhen: The voucher causes an actual school change with materially different instruction.
weakerWhen: The award subsidizes an enrollment that would happen anyway.
absentWhen: No award, school place, eligibility or recorded enrollment change exists.

links.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal stops prospective award authority. It does not erase the award already paid or the pupil prior instruction. A subsequent return to another school needs a household decision and enrollment record.
links.who: Voucher-using pupils and their households, with school/provider-specific effects; nonparticipants cannot be assigned the recipient estimate.
links.lagWhy: The existing12-month lag represents a school year before assessment. Verify the cited voucher study follow-up and treatment group; a state-wide diluted coefficient is not the trial estimate.

links.anchor: D.C. voucher users graduated more (about +12 points for users); few students use them.
links.source: Wolf et al. 2013 (to confirm)
why: A voucher award can make a chosen private-school enrollment feasible.
The household must choose that school and the school must accept the pupil.
The resulting school experience can alter continued attendance and progress.
Graduation occurs only when the pupil completes the applicable requirements.
Bedrock is a funded choice and completed schooling, not a voucher law assigning a diploma.

strongerWhen: A participating pupil attends a school whose completion support differs from the counterfactual school.
weakerWhen: Few eligible pupils participate or the award does not change their school.
absentWhen: The pupil is not a participant or already completed school before exposure.

links.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal can remove funding for future enrollment choices. Previously completed schooling remains; a remaining pupil graduation consequence depends on their later school path.
links.who: Actual voucher participants in the study cohorts; statewide graduation requires measured participation and cohort shares.
links.lagWhy: The existing48-month lag approximates later graduation, but the pupil grade and cited follow-up define when completion could actually change.

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Counties across state borders: turnout 2 to 3 points lower after a right-to-work law passes (about 3% of a 65% turnout), with the Democratic presidential share 3.5 points lower, as unions contact fewer voters
links.source: Feigenbaum, Hertel-Fernandez and Williamson 2018, From the Bargaining Table to the Ballot Box (NBER w24259)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Teacher duty-to-bargain laws had only a modest effect on schooling, consistent with earlier null results on graduation; their measured effect is lower adult earnings for men (3.9%), a measure the game does not keep
links.source: Lovenheim and Willen 2019, AEJ: Economic Policy 11(3)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Connecticut raised the age of juvenile jurisdiction: no loss of deterrence and no rise in crime among the teens it covered
links.source: Loeffler and Chalfin 2017, Criminology and Public Policy 16(1)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: 10% higher teacher pay cuts dropouts 3 to 4%; a state salary floor is assumed to raise average teacher pay about 5%
links.source: Loeb and Page 2000, Review of Economics and Statistics 82(3)
why: An operative salary floor requires a covered public employer to raise under-floor teacher compensation.
The employer changes saved pay terms and pays that amount in actual pay periods.
Higher pay may change retention or recruitment only through a teacher or applicant employment decision.
The changed staffing may alter instruction for the pupils assigned to those teachers.
Bedrock for the direct effect is a legal pay requirement; the graduation continuation needs actual employment, instruction and completion records.

strongerWhen: The floor binds many underpaid covered teachers and resources permit staffing responses.
weakerWhen: Existing salary is already above the floor or the pay rise is small.
absentWhen: A private teacher is outside coverage, the first applicable school year has not begun, or no staffing/instruction change reaches the pupil.

links.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal removes the future legal floor. It does not cut saved teacher pay or revoke a diploma; any staffing response must follow actual later employment terms and decisions.
links.who: Under-floor covered public-school teachers first; only pupils taught by affected staffing can receive an indirect educational consequence.
links.lagWhy: The existing24-month graduation lag is a model approximation. Salary changes begin with the legally operative school year/pay period; staffing and cohort completion need their own dated exposure.

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: States that imposed tax limits in the 1970s and 1980s saw mean math scores fall 5.5 to 6% against other states (about 0.1 standard deviation, or about a tenth fewer eighth graders at the proficient line), most where spending was already low; reading did not change. Today's growth caps are milder than those limits, so the central size is half
links.source: Figlio 1997, Journal of Public Economics 65(3); Downes and Figlio 1997, IRP DP 1142-97

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: The official poverty rate counts cash income before taxes, so a sales tax cannot move it; the real effect is on food insecurity (removing the tax cuts it 3.2% for households under $30,000), a measure the game does not keep
links.source: Zheng, Zhao, Buck, Burney, Kaiser and Wilson 2021, Food Policy 101

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: 217 cities, 1981 to 2015: oversight boards that can investigate and sanction go with lower violent crime; boards that only review go with more
links.source: Ali and Nicholson-Crotty 2021, Public Performance and Management Review

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: From 2018 to 2022, turnout rose about 1 point in districts drawn by long-standing commissions and 5 points in court-drawn ones, and being drawn into a competitive district added about 3 points; the comparison is descriptive, not a controlled study, and presidential turnout is barely touched by district lines
links.source: Brennan Center, The Turnout Effects of Redistricting Institutions; PS: Political Science and Politics 2023 (commissions and competitive elections)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: California's term limits brought no rise, and perhaps a fall, in legislative-race turnout; nothing shows a statewide change
links.source: Nalder 2007, State Politics and Policy Quarterly 7(2)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: The official poverty rate counts cash income before taxes, so an income tax cannot move it; high earners leaving is small
links.source: Census official poverty definition; Young, Varner, Lurie and Prisinzano 2016, American Sociological Review

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: The official poverty rate counts cash income before taxes, so the tax's shape cannot move it
links.source: Census official poverty definition

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: 268 cities, 1997 to 2020: police facial recognition went with lower violent crime and homicide, more so the earlier it was adopted; restricting it gives some of that up, and violence is a small part of all crime
links.source: Johnson, Johnson, Topalli, McCurdy and Wallace 2024, Cities
why: A restriction changes which identification tools government can use.
A covered investigation may use alternatives or lack a face match.
The cited city study reports associations between adoption and crime.
The terminal is an investigative/legal constraint; adoption correlations do not establish the causal reverse of a repeal.
links.conditions: Preserve the existing per-world/per-place draw and recorded range where present. Statutory reach, actual eligible people and service capacity differ; no blanket state coverage is inferred.
links.reverseOnRepeal: Remove or replace the current legal exposure prospectively; enrollment, services, contracts and accumulated outcomes need their own records, not an immediate numerical inverse.
links.who: 268 cities, 1997 to 2020: police facial recognition went with lower violent crime and homicide, more so the earlier it was adopted; restricting it gives some of that up, and violence is a small part of all crime

lagWhy.evidenceLimit: Inherited repository source/anchor read; primary study verification and any new conversion remain Team9 research work.

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: State employment protections raised gay men's wages 2.7% and lowered lesbian women's employment, too small a group to move a state's poverty rate. Enforcing one costs about nothing: the fiscal notes for Utah SB 296 (2015) and West Virginia HB 2266 (2023) each show $0, and the West Virginia commission expected no rise in complaints
links.source: Burn 2018, Journal of Labor Research; Utah Legislative Fiscal Analyst, S.B. 296 fiscal note (3/9/2015); West Virginia Human Rights Commission, HB 2266 fiscal note (1/18/2023)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Inclusionary rules raised prices and slowed building in Boston's suburbs and had no significant effect around San Francisco; the few below-market homes and the slower building roughly cancel
links.source: Schuetz, Meltzer and Been 2011, Urban Studies

links.per: permit required (dropping it raises violent crime about 10%)
links.anchor: States that adopted right-to-carry laws had 13 to 15% more violent crime ten years on than their synthetic controls. The study compares shall-issue with may-issue permits, so it is a proxy for requiring a permit at all
links.source: Donohue, Aneja and Weber 2019, Journal of Empirical Legal Studies 16(2); RAND Science of Gun Policy

links.anchor: New Jersey nearly ended money bail in 2017 with about a 2-point rise in pretrial rearrest and no measurable rise in violent crime
links.source: Anderson, Redcross, Valentine and Miratrix 2019, MDRC

links.anchor: Legal retail cannabis in Colorado and Washington showed no lasting effect on violent crime against comparison states
links.source: Dragone, Prarolo, Vanin and Zanella 2019, Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization 159

links.anchor: Five to nine years after enactment, states with stringent renewable standards cut power-plant sulfur dioxide about 58% and nitrogen oxides about 34%; power plants are a small share of today's fine particles
links.source: Ji, Li, Lee, Luke and Mavrothalassitis 2024, working paper, Cleaner Bills, Cleaner Air

links.anchor: California's cap-and-trade lowered fine-particle emissions at regulated plants 3 to 9% a year from 2012 to 2017; the statewide change in the air is far smaller
links.source: Hernandez-Cortes and Meng 2023, Journal of Public Economics 217

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Removing the grocery tax cuts food insecurity 3.2% among households under $30,000, where most food-insecure households are, so about 2% statewide; only states that taxed groceries in 2024 change
links.source: Zheng, Zhao, Buck, Burney, Kaiser and Wilson 2021, Food Policy 101

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Men schooled under teacher duty-to-bargain laws earn 3.9% less as adults; only exposed cohorts, and only men, so a small statewide share, arriving as they reach working age
links.source: Lovenheim and Willen 2019, AEJ: Economic Policy 11(3)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: State bans on municipal broadband cut access about 4.5% from 2012 to 2018; that measured availability, and subscriptions move less
links.source: Whitacre and Gallardo 2020, Telecommunications Policy 44(9)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: 12.7% of childhood asthma is attributed to gas stoves, from a meta-analysis of associations; a ban reaches only new buildings, so a small part of that over a decade
links.source: Gruenwald, Seals, Knibbs and Hosgood 2022, International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 20(1)

links.anchor: Taxes move few people: even millionaires rarely leave high-tax states
links.source: Young, Varner, Lurie and Prisinzano 2016, American Sociological Review

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0), in basis points
links.anchor: States with strict anti-deficit rules paid 15 to 20 basis points less than states with lax rules on general-obligation bonds, 1973 to 1996; a statute moves a state partway, so 8
links.source: Poterba and Rueben 1999, State Fiscal Institutions and the U.S. Municipal Bond Market (NBER w6237)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0), in basis points
links.anchor: Spreads rose 7 to 15 basis points for each 10% of revenue lost in pension funds in states in the lower half of credit quality. The recorded game estimate is a 3-basis-point reduction, with a -8 to 0 range, because paying the full contribution heads off only part of that observed loss effect (Novy-Marx and Rauh 2012).
links.source: Novy-Marx and Rauh 2012, AEJ: Economic Policy 4(2)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0), in basis points
links.anchor: ESTIMATED FROM THE RECORDED FISCAL-LAW AVERAGE: a minimum reserve balance lowers borrowing cost by 3 basis points, with a -6 to 0 range. The basis is the game's same -3-basis-point estimate for full pension funding; Pew 2017 and Wagner 2004 establish that rainy-day funds raise ratings and lower yields but do not provide basis points per law.
links.source: Pew Charitable Trusts 2017; Wagner 2004

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Transit ridership's elasticity with respect to fares is -0.2 to -0.5 in the first year. A fare falling to zero is read on the semi-log curve the paper recommends for fares near zero, where ridership rises by e to the elasticity: 22% to 65%, 42% at the middle of the range. Long-run elasticities of -0.6 to -0.9 would give more, so this is the first year's effect, held.
links.source: Litman 2025, Transit Price Elasticities and Cross-Elasticities, Victoria Transport Policy Institute, Table 15 and page 9

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Legal adult sales went with 20 to 35% fewer opioid deaths where stores opened, which is 15 to 27% of all overdose deaths at opioids' 76% share (2022). A later check found that result fragile and stores going with more opioid deaths, so the evidence runs both ways and the middle is a small fall. The lag is the months from the law taking effect to the first store opening, averaged over six states: Colorado 13, Washington 19, Michigan 12, Illinois 0, New York 21, Missouri 2 (ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: 11)
links.source: Chan, Burkhardt and Flyr 2020, Economic Inquiry 58(2); Mathur and Ruhm 2023, Journal of Health Economics 88; CDC WONDER 2022 overdose deaths by drug

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: State privacy laws bind only large data holders: the common model reaches a business handling data on 100,000 of the state's consumers, and California's also one with $25 million in revenue. The cost falls on data firms and app makers, which lost investment and apps under Europe's rule, too small a share of a state's workers to move its median earnings
links.source: Va. Code 59.1-576; Cal. Civ. Code 1798.140(d); Jia, Jin and Wagman 2021, Marketing Science 40(4); Janssen, Kesler, Kummer and Waldfogel 2022, NBER Working Paper 30028
why: The law grants qualifying consumers access, correction and deletion rights.

links.anchor: Where federal law let highway money go to transit (1992 to 2006), states spent about 3% of the whole federal-aid highway program on transit, 13% of the flexible part; California put nearly 40% of its flexible money there, and 19 states less than 2%. The same 3% of a state's own highway spending (Census Bureau, 2022: $128.0 billion) is 5.9% of what transit agencies spend to run service (FTA National Transit Database, 2024: $65.6 billion), so service rises about 6% at the average cost per mile. The spread takes 2% to 40% of the flexible part. The lag is a budget cycle and the buses it buys, the most common use GAO found.
links.source: GAO-07-772, Highway and Transit Investments: Flexible Funding Supports State and Local Transportation Priorities (2007); Census Bureau, 2022 Census of Governments: Finance, Table 1 (state highways); FTA National Transit Database 2024 (data.transportation.gov ekg5-frzt, total operating expenses)

links.anchor: Across 269 counties in six Mid-Atlantic states over 50 years, a state or local program that buys farmland development rights cut the county's rate of farmland loss by 40% to 55%. The size is the middle of that range, 47%, and the spread is the paper's own. The lag is one Census of Agriculture period, the step at which the loss was measured, since a program needs years of purchases before its easements hold back development.
links.source: Liu and Lynch 2011, Do Agricultural Land Preservation Programs Reduce Farmland Loss? Evidence from a Propensity Score Matching Estimator, Land Economics 87(2): 183-201; its 40% to 55% as reported in USDA Economic Research Service, Additionality in U.S. Agricultural Conservation and Regulatory Offset Programs, ERR-170 (2014)

links.anchor: Kansas's first Local Enhanced Management Area (Sheridan 6, 2013 to 2017), where irrigators pumped under capped five-year allocations (55 inches of water over five years), cut pumping 31% against a modeled business-as-usual over its first five years (95% interval 21% to 40%). A state law that meters and limits large withdrawals is read as putting such a cap on irrigation pumping; where the cap binds less than it did there, the cut is smaller, so the evidence is provisional. The spread is the paper's interval. The lag is one year, the next irrigation season.
links.source: Deines, Kendall, Butler and Hyndman 2019, Quantifying irrigation adaptation strategies in response to stakeholder-driven groundwater management in the US High Plains Aquifer, Environmental Research Letters 14: 044014 (https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/aafe39)
